paragraphs: Detecting genetic locations associated with traits is difficult when the number of candidate locations greatly exceeds the number of samples. This paper addresses that problem by analyzing related traits together and incorporating information about genomic locations. Such information includes conservation scores and transcription factor binding sites, which can help guide the search for relevant genetic variation.

The authors develop a regularized regression approach within a Bayesian network for multi-task learning. Priors on genetic variants allow the importance of individual predictors to be estimated adaptively. The procedure jointly estimates regression coefficients and predictor weights, so the treatment of a location can reflect both the observed data and its regulatory features. Computation alternates between convex optimization and coordinate descent.

Experiments on simulated data and real yeast data report better eQTL detection than previous methods. These findings support the proposed combination of shared learning across traits and adaptive use of genomic information in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a way to bring those sources of evidence into one estimation procedure.
neurips-2010-adaptive-multi-task-lasso-w.tldr: Adaptive Multi-Task Lasso combines related traits and genomic prior information to improve eQTL detection in simulated and yeast datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies brain responses by grouping both the things people see and the brain locations that respond to them. Stimulus groups become categories, while groups of voxels become functional units. Learning both groupings provides a way to describe how patterns of brain activity relate to structure among the presented stimuli.

The central assumption is that voxels belonging to the same functional unit respond similarly to stimuli within a category. A nonparametric hierarchical model captures variation in these units across individuals. It also explicitly connects brain activations to the time courses measured by fMRI, making the observed signals part of the account of category-dependent responses.

The authors derive a variational inference algorithm that learns stimulus categories, functional units, and activation probabilities for each unit-category pairing. Applied to an object-recognition fMRI study, the method finds meaningful and consistent groupings of both stimuli and voxels. The result supports jointly organizing the stimulus and brain sides of the data while accommodating differences between subjects.
neurips-2010-categories-and-functional-u.tldr: A hierarchical model jointly discovers stimulus categories and functional brain units while accounting for variation across individuals.

paragraphs: Regularized Information Maximization, or RIM, addresses how to learn a probabilistic classifier when examples have no labels. It jointly assigns data to clusters and trains a classifier to distinguish those clusters. This makes the grouping of the data and the rule for predicting group membership parts of a single learning problem.

Its information-theoretic objective balances three considerations: separation between classes, the distribution of examples among classes, and classifier complexity. The framework can express prior beliefs about relative class sizes and can use partial labels when some supervision is available. It also accommodates different likelihood functions, allowing the same broad approach to support different probabilistic classifiers.

The paper develops an instance based on unsupervised, multi-class kernelized logistic regression. Empirical evaluation reports better performance than existing methods on several real datasets and finds RIM effective for model selection. These results support using the balance among separation, class sizes, and complexity to guide both clustering and the choice of a predictive model.
neurips-2010-discriminative-clustering-b.tldr: RIM jointly learns clusters and a probabilistic classifier by balancing class separation, class sizes, and model complexity.

paragraphs: Relational data describe connections between objects, such as relationships among people in a social network. Those connections can change as groups appear, disappear, split, or merge. This paper proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing such evolving group structure, with communities in social networks serving as an example of the kind of pattern it seeks to capture.

The model represents observed relationships between individual objects through relationships between clusters of objects. It extends the infinite Hidden Markov model to track changes in relational structure over time. The number of clusters is estimated alongside their temporal evolution, bringing the questions of how many groups exist and how their structure changes into the same analysis.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the model's usefulness. The contribution is a framework that treats changing cluster structure as part of the phenomenon to be modeled. This gives the analysis a way to describe additions, deletions, and reorganizations of groups through a shared probabilistic representation.
neurips-2010-dynamic-infinite-relational.tldr: A dynamic relational model jointly estimates evolving object clusters and their number, including changes such as splits and merges.

paragraphs: This paper addresses extracting particular white matter structures from three-dimensional diffusion tensor brain images. Such segmentation supports studies that compare structures across groups, including groups defined by disease. Expert-guided segmentation can provide the desired regions, but repeating that interaction across large datasets is tedious.

The proposed method summarizes expert-segmented examples into an epitome of a target region. This epitome is a histogram of feature descriptors: a compact account of the kinds of image features that characterize the structure. When segmenting a new image, the algorithm adds constraints encouraging the extracted foreground to agree with that histogram. Expert knowledge therefore influences the overall composition of the selected region.

The authors develop combinatorial approximation algorithms for incorporating these constraints into Markov Random Field segmentation, drawing on image co-segmentation results. They analyze solution quality and present promising experimental evidence that many neuroscience structures can be extracted reliably from three-dimensional volumes. The approach connects reusable region-level guidance with a formal segmentation procedure.
neurips-2010-epitome-driven-3-d-diffusio.tldr: Feature histograms learned from expert segmentations guide automated extraction of specific white matter structures from three-dimensional brain images.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how prediction performance changes with the amount of training data. This paper studies Gaussian process regression using Bayes error averaged over datasets of a given size. Calculating that average is generally difficult, so the authors focus on discrete input spaces whose similarities are represented by a graph.

The method translates the relevant belief propagation equations into equations for an ensemble of graphs. It produces accurate predictions and is expected to become exact for large graphs from a broad range of random graph ensembles. That expectation applies to graphs with arbitrary degree distributions in which each node connects to only a finite number of others.

The authors demonstrate prediction accuracy for Poisson, or Erdos-Renyi, graphs and regular random graphs. They also examine when and why earlier learning-curve approximations fail. The contribution is a way to connect average regression performance to the structure of graph-based input domains, with a stated large-graph regime supporting the prospect of exact predictions.
neurips-2010-exact-learning-curves-for-g.tldr: Graph-ensemble belief propagation predicts Gaussian process learning curves accurately and is expected to become exact for suitable large random graphs.

paragraphs: This paper connects the timing of neural spikes to fractional differentiation. Earlier experimental work had suggested that firing rates could have this interpretation when changing signals induce adaptation. The authors extend the interpretation to the spike train itself, provided that the underlying neural signal is approximated as a sum of power-law kernels.

A standard threshold-based spiking neuron can produce this approximation when equipped with a suitable refractory response. Empirically, the representation benefits signals with slowly changing components, including long-memory self-similar signals. For those signals, it typically needs fewer than half as many spikes as comparable exponentially decaying kernels to achieve similar signal-to-noise ratios.

The paper also considers how a receiving neuron could decode the spikes. Power-law kernels can be approximated accurately through weighted sums or cascades of exponentials. Adjusting the decoding weights then provides a direct way to filter the reconstructed signal over time. Together, the results connect a conditional mathematical interpretation of spikes with efficient encoding and adjustable temporal decoding.
neurips-2010-fractionally-predictive-spi.tldr: Power-law signal representations give spike trains a fractional-derivative interpretation and empirically encode certain slowly varying signals with substantially fewer spikes.

paragraphs: Matching functional brain areas across people is difficult because their positions and sizes vary. Tumors can make the problem especially pronounced by reorganizing functional systems. Anatomical alignment then has limited value for identifying corresponding functional areas or locating active regions that have shifted from their usual positions.

The authors propose aligning brains in a space defined by patterns of functional interaction. Each brain is embedded in a functional map reflecting connectivity during an fMRI experiment. The maps are registered to one another, and the resulting matches are transferred back to the original brains. This makes connectivity patterns the basis for establishing correspondence between regions.

Preliminary results from a language fMRI experiment suggest improved functional matches across subjects. The apparent advantage is particularly pronounced for people with tumors affecting language areas and causing spatial reorganization. The findings support the possibility that functional interaction geometry can help locate corresponding areas when anatomy alone provides an incomplete guide.
neurips-2010-functional-geometry-alignme.tldr: Aligning connectivity-based brain maps shows preliminary improvements in matching functional areas, especially when tumors have reorganized language regions.

paragraphs: System identification asks what can be learned about a system's internal parameters when its input and output are both observed. This paper applies that question to dendritic processing in a neural circuit. The goal is to recover the processing that occurs before the circuit generates spikes, using the relationship between an incoming signal and spike-associated timing.

The assumed circuit consists of a linear dendritic filter followed by a spiking neuron model. Its input is an analog signal restricted to the space of bandlimited functions, and its output is a time sequence associated with the spike train. These assumptions define the mathematical setting in which the hidden filter is identified.

The authors derive an identification algorithm and show that the filter's kernel can be reconstructed with arbitrary precision within this setting. The result gives a formal route from observed input and spike timing to the dendritic filter itself. Its scope rests on the specified linear-filter cascade and bandlimited input model.
neurips-2010-identifying-dendritic-proce.tldr: An identification algorithm reconstructs a linear dendritic filter with arbitrary precision in a specified spiking circuit with bandlimited inputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies incomplete binary matrices that change over time, together with documents describing entities along at least one matrix axis. Legislative voting provides the motivating example: entries represent votes, and documents contain the associated legislation. The aim is to uncover hidden structure and relationships represented by latent features on both matrix axes.

The proposed Bayesian framework combines incomplete-matrix analysis with topic modeling. Joint analysis lets patterns in the documents inform the matrices and lets matrix structure inform the interpretation of the documents. It also creates the possibility of predicting a matrix entry from an associated document alone, such as predicting a vote using the text of legislation.

Inference is performed through an efficient Gibbs sampling procedure. The framework is demonstrated on all voting data and available legislative documents from the stated 220-year history of the United States Senate and House of Representatives. The contribution is a shared treatment of evolving binary relationships and text, allowing complementary evidence to enter one analysis.
neurips-2010-joint-analysis-of-time-evol.tldr: A Bayesian model jointly analyzes evolving binary matrices and documents, enabling each source to inform the other and potentially support text-only predictions.

paragraphs: Visual recognition depends strongly on how small image regions are represented. This paper reinterprets orientation histograms, including those used in SIFT and HOG, as a particular kind of match kernel between image patches. That equivalence provides a mathematical starting point for constructing a broader family of image descriptors.

The authors introduce three types of match kernels that measure patch similarity and use kernel principal component analysis to turn them into compact, low-dimensional features. The framework can build patch representations from pixel attributes such as gradients, colors, and local binary patterns. This connects the choice of local image information to a common procedure for producing usable descriptors.

The paper reports that these kernel descriptors outperform carefully tuned features, including SIFT and deep belief networks, in its evaluations. Superior performance is reported on Scene-15, Caltech-101, CIFAR10, and CIFAR10-ImageNet. The results support the practical value of designing patch similarities first and then deriving compact features through the kernel framework.
neurips-2010-kernel-descriptors-for-visu.tldr: Kernel descriptors turn pixel attributes into compact image-patch features through match kernels and outperform several established representations on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models for scene understanding must both discover hidden topics and learn to predict scene categories. The paper identifies a problem with existing maximum-likelihood training schemes: they can make prediction-model learning independent of topic discovery. That separation can produce an imbalanced prediction rule, weakening the connection between the learned representation and classification.

The proposed method combines maximum-margin and maximum-likelihood learning in a joint objective. This closely couples discovery of the latent topics with estimation of the prediction model. The authors solve the optimization efficiently through variational expectation-maximization, which repeatedly solves an online loss-augmented support vector machine problem as part of the training procedure.

Experiments demonstrate advantages of the large-margin approach on an eight-category sports dataset and the 67-class MIT indoor scene dataset. The reported findings support training the representation and prediction rule together for these scene-categorization tasks. The contribution is an integrated learning method that makes classification requirements part of the process that discovers latent scene structure.
neurips-2010-large-margin-learning-of-up.tldr: Joint maximum-margin and maximum-likelihood training couples latent topic discovery with scene classification and improves results on two scene datasets.

paragraphs: The head and outer ears filter sounds differently depending on their source location. These head-related transfer functions provide localization cues, but they change over an organism's lifetime. A neural system therefore needs a way to learn location cues from the filtered sounds it actually hears, since the filtering functions are not directly available through experience.

This paper proposes a spiking neural network that extracts synchrony patterns specific to sound locations. A simple supervised algorithm learns the relationship between those patterns and locations from example sounds. The model begins without prior knowledge of the head-related transfer functions, so the mapping must be acquired through the examples themselves.

After learning, the model accurately localizes new sounds in both azimuth and elevation. It also handles the difficult distinction between sounds arriving from the front and the back. The results show that learned synchrony patterns can support spatial hearing in this model, connecting experience with spike-based representations of sound location.
neurips-2010-learning-to-localise-sounds.tldr: A spiking network learns sound locations from synchrony patterns without prior knowledge of ear filtering, including front-versus-back distinctions.

paragraphs: Models combining first-order logic with probabilistic graphical representations can contain repeated structure. Lifted inference uses that structure to make probabilistic calculations more efficient. The paper describes earlier approaches as starting from familiar inference algorithms, such as variable elimination or belief propagation, and adapting them to exploit repetitions in the model.

The authors instead begin with the logical representation itself. They define rules that inspect its logical structure to identify models for which exact inference can be performed efficiently. This changes the focus from accelerating a chosen inference procedure to recognizing features of a model that make efficient exact calculation possible.

The rules establish several new tractable classes that the existing techniques considered in the paper could not solve efficiently. The contribution therefore includes both a different route to inference and an expanded account of which models admit efficient solutions. The result concerns the classes identified by those rules, giving a structural basis for recognizing tractability in combined logical and probabilistic representations.
neurips-2010-lifted-inference-seen-from-.tldr: Rules based on logical structure identify new classes of probabilistic models that permit efficient exact inference.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves labels with interconnected parts, making both learning and inference difficult for general graph structures. This paper asks whether the distribution of training inputs can help overcome that computational difficulty. Its answer is conditional: a sufficiently rich input distribution can make it possible to learn through an alternative to the otherwise intractable approach.

The proposed pseudo-max method is similar in spirit to pseudo-likelihood. The authors establish consistency for their approach, connecting its computational strategy to a statistical guarantee. The richness requirement matters because the paper's claim is that the difficulty can be circumvented when the inputs provide enough structure for the method to work.

The empirical results show performance comparable to exact methods when training sets are sufficiently large. This supports a relationship between data availability and the amount of inference needed during learning: more examples can make the proposed alternative effective. Both the theoretical and experimental conclusions retain their qualifications, involving input-distribution richness and sufficiently large training sets, respectively.
neurips-2010-more-data-means-less-infere.tldr: Pseudo-max can circumvent difficult structured-learning inference under a sufficiently rich input distribution and empirically match exact methods with enough training data.

paragraphs: Active learning concerns how many labeled examples a learner needs when it can choose which examples to query. Much theory assumes realizability, meaning that the available model class can perfectly represent the labeling rule. This paper studies the non-realizable case with multiple views of the data, addressing a setting where that ideal assumption does not hold.

Under unbounded Tsybakov noise, the authors prove that multi-view active learning can achieve a label requirement that grows logarithmically with inverse target error, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. They contrast this possibility with the single-view setting, where the best possible improvement is polynomial. The logarithmic result is a possible multi-view rate, rather than a guarantee for every such setting.

For the general multi-view setting, they establish a bound proportional to inverse target error, again up to logarithmic factors. Its exponent is independent of the Tsybakov noise parameter, unlike earlier polynomial bounds. Together, the results characterize how multiple views can change label requirements even when perfect realizability is unavailable.
neurips-2010-multi-view-active-learning-.tldr: The paper proves improved multi-view active-learning label bounds under unbounded Tsybakov noise without assuming realizability.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an efficient way to estimate natural policy gradients for control tasks using parameter-based exploration. Exploration samples directly in the policy's parameter space. The learning procedure therefore combines variation in policy parameters with a natural-gradient calculation, addressing how to make that calculation computationally practical in the proposed setting.

The defining computational feature is use of the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix. The authors report that their algorithm has the same computational cost as conventional policy-gradient methods, while the previous natural-gradient approaches they discuss have prohibitive costs. The contribution is thus a particular combination of exploration and gradient estimation that makes exact Fisher-based calculation affordable.

Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms several policy-gradient methods. Those findings provide empirical support for the algorithm alongside its stated computational advantage. Taken together, the results indicate that parameter-based exploration can support an effective natural policy-gradient procedure without increasing computational cost beyond the conventional policy-gradient comparison made in the paper.
neurips-2010-natural-policy-gradient-met.tldr: Parameter-based exploration enables exact Fisher-based natural policy-gradient estimation at conventional policy-gradient cost, with better results in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In a slate bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses a fixed-size subset of available actions and observes rewards only for the selected actions. Online advertising and news selection motivate this setting. The objective is to keep cumulative reward close to that of the best slate that could be chosen after seeing the full sequence.

The paper develops efficient algorithms for both unordered and ordered slates. Their regret grows on the order of the square root of the number of rounds, with constants depending on the particular problem. Because this growth is slower than the number of rounds, the bound implies that regret per round decreases as the interaction continues.

The authors also consider access to policies that recommend slates each round. They obtain square-root regret bounds for competing with the best recommendation policy as well. The algorithms combine multiplicative weight updates with relative entropy projections, extending a common online-learning update technique to the constraints imposed by choosing whole slates.
neurips-2010-non-stochastic-bandit-slate.tldr: Efficient slate-selection algorithms achieve square-root regret against the best fixed slate or recommending policy with feedback only on selected actions.

paragraphs: This paper derives likelihood-ratio policy gradients from an importance-sampling perspective. The derivation reveals two ways that these reinforcement-learning methods underuse experience. They use observations to estimate only the gradient of expected return at the current policy parameters, and they restrict that estimation to experience collected under the current policy.

The proposed policy-search method uses both observations to broaden the role of past data. It seeks a more complete estimate of expected return and draws on experience from past policies as well as the current one. It also introduces generalized baselines, extending the baseline techniques commonly used in policy-gradient methods.

The algorithm outperforms standard likelihood-ratio policy-gradient algorithms on several testbeds. These results support the practical value of the proposed experience reuse in the evaluated problems. The conceptual contribution is the connection between importance sampling and policy gradients: it exposes where an established update rule leaves information unused and motivates a search procedure designed to use more of it.
neurips-2010-on-a-connection-between-imp.tldr: An importance-sampling view motivates a policy-search method that uses past experience more fully and outperforms standard likelihood-ratio gradients on several testbeds.

paragraphs: Cortical circuits expand relatively few sensory input channels into activity across many neurons, producing an over-complete representation. Those neurons are connected through sparse lateral synapses. This paper proposes that the combination of expanded representation and sparse recurrent connectivity may help a percept persist after an incoming stimulus has been represented.

The authors study a family of networks in which each neuron's receptive field is re-expressed through its outgoing connections. They call this connectivity arrangement REceptive FIeld REcombination, or REFIRE. For this family, they demonstrate that the represented percept can remain unchanged even while neural activity changes. Persistence therefore concerns the information represented by the network, not a requirement that every neuron maintain constant activity.

The paper suggests that sparse REFIRE networks may act as high-dimensional integrators and may provide a biologically plausible model of local cortical circuitry. These are proposed implications of the architecture. The demonstrated result is the possibility of preserving a percept under changing activity when the specified connectivity relationship holds.
neurips-2010-over-complete-representatio.tldr: REFIRE connectivity allows an over-complete recurrent network to preserve a represented percept even as its neural activity changes.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when the underlying state is high-dimensional or only partly observable. Methods then depend on features, and their success can hinge on whether those features preserve useful information. This paper considers a large collection of features whose individual contributions to estimating future value may each be limited.

Predictive State Temporal Difference learning, or PSTD, combines linear temporal-difference learning with subspace identification. It finds a linear compression that reduces the large feature set to a smaller one while preserving the maximum amount of predictive information. It then uses a Bellman recursion to estimate a value function from that representation, connecting predictive feature selection with reinforcement-learning estimation.

The authors prove statistical consistency, use experiments to illustrate the algorithm's properties, and demonstrate its potential on a difficult optimal-stopping problem. They also relate PSTD to earlier reinforcement-learning and subspace-identification approaches. The contribution is a coordinated way to compress abundant features and use the retained predictive information for value estimation.
neurips-2010-predictive-state-temporal-d.tldr: PSTD compresses large feature sets to preserve predictive information, then uses temporal-difference learning for statistically consistent value estimation.

paragraphs: Random Projection Trees divide a data space into progressively smaller cells and can adapt to the data's intrinsic dimensionality. This paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of two versions, RPTree-Max and RPTree-Mean. Its focus is how the geometry of the data influences the behavior of these partitioning structures.

For RPTree-Max, the authors prove a near-optimal bound on how many tree levels are needed to shrink cell size by a chosen factor of at least two. They also establish a packing lemma for the structure. These results sharpen the account of how its partitions become smaller and how the resulting cells are organized geometrically.

The final result connects low-dimensional manifolds to bounded Local Covariance Dimension. That connection establishes that RPTree-Mean adapts to manifold dimension as well. The contribution is theoretical: it extends the guarantees for these existing data structures and links their adaptive behavior to another important description of low-dimensional structure in data.
neurips-2010-random-projection-trees-rev.tldr: New proofs sharpen RPTree-Max partition guarantees and establish that RPTree-Mean adapts to manifold dimension.

paragraphs: Large genetic studies must relate many genetic variants, biomarkers, and traits while accounting for noise and unobserved confounders. Sparse Instrumental Variables, or SPIV, provides a probabilistic framework for this setting. It adapts sparse linear regression methods to infer causal structure in richer networks that include latent variables.

The approach is motivated by using genotypes as instruments for studying causal associations between biomarkers and outcomes. It is designed to avoid common restrictive assumptions of instrumental-variable methods. The framework may screen for potentially interesting genotype-trait and biomarker-trait associations. When biomarkers are gene transcripts, it can also support fine mapping of quantitative trait loci found through genetic linkage studies.

The paper applies the method to liver gene-transcript levels and plasma HDL cholesterol in sequenced mice from a heterogeneous stock, using about 100,000 genetic instruments and 47,000 transcripts. The proposed screening applications may help investigate biomarkers as possible proxy endpoints for early clinical trials. Those implications remain potential uses of the framework, rather than demonstrated clinical validation.
neurips-2010-sparse-instrumental-variabl.tldr: SPIV combines sparse modeling and genetic instruments to investigate biomarker-trait relationships in large studies with noise and hidden confounders.

paragraphs: Estimating an undirected graph from high-dimensional data requires choosing how strongly to regularize the model. That choice affects which edges are retained. StARS selects the regularization level using stability under random sampling, seeking the least regularization that makes the estimated graph both sparse and reproducible.

This gives the selection rule an interpretation that requires essentially no conditions: retain a relatively lightly regularized graph while demanding sampling stability. The theoretical recovery result has additional requirements. Under mild conditions, StARS includes all true edges with high probability as graph size grows with sample size. This partial sparsistency guarantee concerns retaining true edges; it does not establish exact recovery of the entire edge set.

The authors compare StARS with cross-validation, AIC, BIC, and other competing selection procedures on synthetic data and a real microarray dataset. StARS outperforms all the compared procedures in those evaluations. The paper thus combines a stability-based selection principle, a qualified edge-retention guarantee, and empirical evidence in high-dimensional graph estimation.
neurips-2010-stability-approach-to-regul.tldr: StARS chooses graph regularization through sampling stability and, under mild conditions, retains all true edges with high probability.

paragraphs: Latent force models describe related dynamical systems through differential equations driven by hidden functions. Gaussian process priors express uncertainty about those functions, and the resulting interactions are encoded in a covariance function. This paper applies that framework to determining robot motor primitives, the movement components that motivate its segmentation problem.

The authors extend the model to switch between latent driving functions and, potentially, between different dynamical systems. Switching accommodates discontinuities in either the dynamics or the hidden forces. The resulting representation can capture discrete changes and nonlinearities in robot movements while retaining the connection between differential-equation structure and uncertain latent inputs.

Illustrative examples use synthetic data and striking movements recorded with a Barrett WAM robot serving as a haptic input device. These examples show the model in the movement setting that motivates it. The authors also anticipate applications to human motion capture and systems biology, presenting those domains as expected extensions of a broader approach to changing dynamical systems.
neurips-2010-switched-latent-force-model.tldr: Switching latent force models represent robot movements with changing hidden forces or dynamics, illustrated on synthetic data and recorded striking movements.
